entities.name: François Arnaud
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
François Arnaud (1721–1784) was a distinguished French clergyman, philologist, and man of letters whose intellectual contributions significantly shaped aesthetic and literary discourse during the Enlightenment. Born in Carpentras, he rose to prominence within Parisian intellectual circles, becoming a member of the prestigious Académie française in 1771. His career exemplified the intersection of classical scholarship, clerical duties, and a fervent engagement with contemporary cultural debates, placing him at the heart of 18th-century French erudition.

Arnaud's most notable contribution to public intellectual life was his impassioned involvement in the 'Querelle des Gluckistes et Piccinnistes' (1777–1779), a profound debate on the future of French opera. As a staunch defender of Christoph Willibald Gluck's operatic reforms, Arnaud published several influential essays, including 'Lettre sur la musique' (1777), arguing for dramatic truth and emotional power over traditional Italianate melodic ornamentation. Beyond this musical controversy, he was a respected Hellenist, translating and commenting on classical Greek texts, and contributing extensively to literary criticism through articles in the *Journal étranger* and *Gazette littéraire de l'Europe*.

His advocacy for Gluck's principles helped solidify a new direction for French opera, emphasizing dramatic coherence and the synthesis of music and text, which profoundly influenced subsequent composers like Hector Berlioz. Arnaud's broader critical work contributed to the Enlightenment's re-evaluation of classical antiquity and the development of modern literary aesthetics, fostering a climate where reasoned argument and refined taste were paramount. His intellectual rigor and willingness to engage in major cultural battles left an indelible mark on the era's intellectual landscape.
